youtube.title: Orphan Tsunami: How Japan Recorded a Quake It Never Felt
youtube.description:
The orphan tsunami of 1700 hit Japan's coast with no earthquake anyone felt. So where did the wave come from? As California braces for record tides this week, here is the strangest wave the Pacific ever sent.

In January 1700, waves swept away houses in the Japanese town of Kuwagasaki, and a fire destroyed even more, yet nobody in Japan had felt the ground shake. Three centuries later, scientists matched those samurai and village records with ghost forests of drowned cedars in Washington, tree rings that stop in 1699, and Native oral histories of a winter night flood. Together they point to a magnitude 9 Cascadia earthquake at about 9 at night on January 26, 1700.

Subscribe to Stickstory for one strange true story a day. Could you sleep through a quake on the other side of the ocean? Tell me in the comments!

scenes.text: A tsunami hit Japan with no earthquake.
scenes.visual: Night on an Edo-period Japanese fishing shore: a towering woodblock-style wave with claw-like foam surges in and curls over two tiled-roof houses and a bent pine under the moon; a villager runs from it between the wave and the first house.

scenes.text: In 1700, homes washed away, but no one felt a tremor.
scenes.visual: Close-up inside a Japanese house at night: a giant wave rears up behind the shoji paper; on 'washed' sea water floods in under the shoji across the floor around the tray; the tea bowl's surface stays dead flat and the paper lantern hangs perfectly still beside a red dashed plumb line on 'tremor'.

scenes.text: So where did this orphan wave come from?
scenes.visual: A Japanese record scroll unrolls on a low desk, columns of brush writing appear right to left with a small brush drawing of a wave; on 'orphan' a red brush circle rings the wave entry; on 'come' a big red handwritten 'ORPHAN WAVE?' pops in.

Close-up push on an old ink map of the Pacific Northwest coast: the red barbed Cascadia fault runs offshore; the fez host stands on North America's green land, reaching left to the fault; 'NORTH AMERICA' runs up the land; on 'ocean' wave fronts roll out across the empty sea and a big red '?' pops over the water.

scenes.text: In Washington, cedars died as the land sank,
scenes.visual: A stand of green, living western red cedars on a tidal flat; on 'died' the ground drops, the tide floods in between the trunks, the needles wither and fall and silver dead snags with broken tops are left in salt water; handwritten 'GHOST FOREST'; on 'sank' a red arrow points down.

scenes.text: and their last rings end in 1699.
scenes.visual: Close-up of a big dead cedar stump on the tidal flat, its cut face with growth rings drawing themselves outward from the centre; on '1699' the outermost ring flashes red and a tag reading '1699' pins onto it.

scenes.text: And Native stories there tell of a winter night flood.
scenes.visual: Winter night on the Pacific Northwest coast, snow falling: an elder in a woven cedar-bark hat sits by a fire telling two listeners a story; the fire's smoke draws a row of plank houses, and on 'sea' a great wave rears up in the smoke over them; the listeners flinch.

scenes.text: So run the wave's timing backwards,
scenes.visual: Wide old ink map of the North Pacific, ocean edge to edge: a gold flash at Japan's coast, then the wave fronts run backwards across the whole ocean and shrink into the red Cascadia fault off North America.

scenes.text: and you get a magnitude nine quake, about nine at night, January 26.
scenes.visual: Close-up on the Cascadia fault off North America: on 'magnitude' a gold burst explodes on the fault, the coast shakes and a red 'M 9' box slams in; on 'night' a clock springs in on the land beside the burst and spins to nine with a '9 PM' box; on 'January' a red 'JAN 26, 1700'.

scenes.text: Japan kept the receipt for a quake it never felt.
scenes.visual: The Japanese record scroll lies open on the desk; the fez host beside it points at the wave entry, a red seal stamp reading '1700' slams onto the scroll on 'receipt', and the host shrugs with a grin.

scenes.text: Subscribe for a true story like this every day.
scenes.visual: The ghost forest at night: silver dead cedar snags stand in the moonlit tide, the tide line creeps up and heaves between the trunks, marsh grass sways; the camera pulls slowly back.
